previous.passage: Warm yeast, wet flour, and the hiss of the tandoor filled the Samarkand bakery long before dawn. Darius arrived each morning at four, though Aydin paid him only for six, and he swept the floor before she could ask. Neither of them spoke of the winter her husband had lent Darius's mother the money for a surgery, or of the fact that it had never been repaid. When he lifted the heaviest trays, she pretended not to notice. When she slipped an extra round of bread into his satchel, wrapped in a cloth embroidered with her husband's initials, he pretended the same. Once, he began to say something about his mother, and Aydin handed him a sack of sesame seeds before he could finish. Through the window, the blue dome of the mosque slowly took shape against the brightening sky.

previous.passage: We waited on the bench nearest the Havana ferry ramp, Father Emiliano in his faded cassock and I, Cleotilde, with a ticket my cousin had bought me to leave by morning. A thick mooring rope lay coiled at our feet, salt-stiff and frayed where it had rubbed the pier for years. I had not been to Mass in a decade, and I told him so, as if he did not already know. He only nodded at the rope. Every boat that docks here, he said, gets tied with that same line, and it never seems to break. When the gangway lowered, a deckhand looped the rope around a post, and the ferry strained against it, groaning, held fast. I folded my ticket into a smaller square. Even after I stood, my eyes kept returning to that worn rope, knotted so many times it had stopped looking like rope at all.

previous.passage: Milena held the dustpan while her mother swept, as she had every Saturday since she was nine. Marlon's barbershop on Brīvības Street closed at six, and her mother, who had cut hair there for twenty years, never let anyone else sweep up. Tonight they were supposed to be choosing wedding napkins, and the catalog lay open on a barber chair, but the broom kept moving in its old pattern: under the mirrors, around the coat rack, toward the door. Brown curls, gray tufts, a child's blond fringe. You'll have your own floors soon, her mother said, not looking up. Milena tipped the pan into the bin. Then she took the broom from her mother's hands and finished the last corner herself, the way she had seen it done a thousand times. Marlon, counting the till, pretended not to watch. Her mother sat down at last and turned a page of the catalog.

previous.passage:
Three rules of the theater in the off-season:
no films, no tickets, no one asks why you came.
Nandi sat in row nine in his pressed uniform,
his transfer papers folded inside his cap,
and Neema, his sister, swept popcorn husks
from a Nairobi rainy season months gone.
Above them the screen hung blank and white,
a field no one had walked across yet.
He had watched worse things than films on other walls.
She flicked the projector on by accident,
and light poured out with nothing in it,
just dust turning slowly in the beam.
He did not ask her to switch it off.
He stood, walked to the stage, and laid his palm
flat against the empty screen,
as if it were warm, as if it might hold
whatever he decided to put there.
Neema kept sweeping. The cap stayed on the seat.

previous.passage: Who gives a widow a shovel for her seventy-fifth birthday? Zawadi had asked herself that for a week, ever since Theo arrived with the long box tied in green ribbon. Since his grandfather's death she had not left the flat, and she suspected the gift was a polite way of telling her to stop sitting in the dark and find some useful chore. So the shovel stood in the corner of the kitchen like an accusation, and each time she passed it, she looked away. On Sunday Theo came back and took her by the arm to the community garden above the Marseille harbor. In the far bed, under a fig tree, a small wooden sign carried his grandfather's name. He kept this plot for forty years, Theo said. Nobody else should dig it. Zawadi stood very still, then held out her hand for the shovel he had carried up the hill.

previous.passage: Some alliances arrive disguised. I had spent a month dreading the afternoon Dwayne's aunt Kemoy would join our wedding planning at the salt-water pool in Port of Spain, where my mother and I did our best thinking with our feet in the water. Kemoy had opinions, everyone warned me, and she had opposed the engagement. I rehearsed polite refusals. When she arrived, she criticized the guest list, the menu, the color of the tablecloths, and I felt my mother stiffen beside me. Then Kemoy pulled a folded paper from her bag: the name of a caterer who owed her a favor, a cousin with a free hall, a band that played for half price. She had not come to oppose us.
